# Welcome {.unnumbered}

As the name implies, this is an open access textbook on personality psychology. I wrote it because I wanted a free resource for my students and couldn't find one I liked. The goal is to give an up-to-date introduction to personality research from a scientific perspective.

I start with a chapter on frameworks I think are useful for orienting our questions about personality ([Ch. 1](01-foundational-frameworks.qmd)). Then I pay some lip service to historical figures like Freud and Jung, who had a lot to say about personality without much data to back it up ([Ch. 2](02-past-perspectives.qmd)). With that out of the way, we turn to the perspectives that largely inform contemporary approaches---and to current models like the Big Five and HEXACO, which we use as a reference point for the rest of the book ([Ch. 3](03-contemporary-perspectives.qmd)). After working through some matters of measurement ([Ch. 4](04-measurement-matters.qmd)), and glossing over a debate that wasted literal decades in psychology ([Ch. 5](05-personality-power.qmd)), we shift to a more topical approach.

From there we examine how evolutionary theory helps us understand personality ([Ch. 6](06-evolution-and-personality.qmd)), and what cutting-edge genetics ([Ch. 7](07-genetics-and-personality.qmd)) and neuroscience ([Ch. 8](08-physiology-and-personality.qmd)) research can tell us about it. We look at how personality relates to other psychological phenomena like emotions ([Ch. 9](09-emotions-and-personality.qmd)) and motivations ([Ch. 10](10-motivation-and-personality.qmd)), how personality develops ([Ch. 11](11-development-and-personality.qmd)), and the interplay between personality and culture ([Ch. 12](12-culture-and-personality.qmd)). Finally, we ask whether and how personality can be voluntarily changed ([Ch. 13](13-personality-change.qmd)).

This is meant to be a living document. I plan to update it every so often as new research advances or changes our understanding of these topics. Corrections and suggestions are welcome by [email](mailto:pdurkee@csufresno.edu), or you can suggest a change directly: every chapter has an **Edit this page** link that opens the text on GitHub, where you can fix a typo, reword something, or add a study you think belongs. It takes a free GitHub account and nothing else, and GitHub walks you through sending it to me. If you would rather flag something than fix it, **Report an issue** does that. I hope you find it useful!
